effect_mechanism: Restoring forest rebuilds the habitat that native species depend on, and the gain is moderate overall. A meta-analysis across 221 study landscapes found forest restoration enhances biodiversity by 15–84% and vegetation structure by 36–77% compared with degraded ecosystems [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles16_1], and a meta-analysis of terrestrial restoration found restored sites had 20% higher mean biodiversity than unrestored sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_atkinson22_1]. Natural regeneration outperforms active planting: restoration success for biodiversity was 34 to 56% higher [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles17_1]. In Brazil restored areas, regardless of technique, show higher diversity than agricultural land and pasture [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jakovac24_2], and tree species richness rises with time since disturbance [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_1]. Woody species richness in Senegal exclosures rose from 27 species at 1 year to 51 at 5 and 12 years [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1], and Ethiopian authors credit afforestation and area closures with improving biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2]. Compilers in Afghanistan, Bangladesh and India report animal, plant and habitat diversity rising under protection and regeneration [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_7460_2024_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_4372_2019_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_5243_2019_plant_diversity], and protection and community management retain forest cover [ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1]. A global study of natural climate solutions, citing an earlier assessment, lists biodiversity habitat among reforestation's well-demonstrated co-benefits [ev_biodiversity_outcome_griscom17_2].
conditionality: The sub-practices do not all agree. One review names a harm: where forests can regenerate naturally, reforestation by tree planting can reduce biodiversity benefits if the species or management chosen do not provide suitable habitat [ev_biodiversity_outcome_williams24_1]. Some units found no gain: abundance in restored systems often does not differ from pasture and agricultural land [ev_biodiversity_outcome_jakovac24_3], there was no clear-cut evidence that a Vietnamese forest project helped biodiversity [ev_biodiversity_outcome_ieg18_1], and management transfers in Madagascar remained superficial while clearing continued [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2]. The terrestrial restoration meta-analysis pools forest with non-forest ecosystems and natural with assisted restoration [ev_biodiversity_outcome_atkinson22_1]. Many supporting units are compiler ratings or forest-cover change standing in for biodiversity, and the Ethiopian result is a qualitative report from a bundled watershed programme [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2]. The global co-benefit listing is second-hand and gives no size [ev_biodiversity_outcome_griscom17_2].

effect_mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings, closing land to cutting and grazing and protecting forest strongly raises biodiversity. In Senegal, woody species richness in village exclosures rose from 27 species in a 1-year exclosure to 51 species in 5- and 12-year exclosures, more than 52% higher [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1]. In an Ethiopian watershed, the authors report improved biodiversity through afforestation and area closures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2]. Compilers report that migratory animals and birds returned to protected land in Afghanistan [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_7460_2024_animal_diversity], that habitat and animal diversity increased with canopy cover and tree density in Bangladesh [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_4372_2019_habitat_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_4372_2019_animal_diversity], and that Indian community forests provide more water and habitat for small animals and birds, with plant diversity up through better moisture, soil and microclimate [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_5243_2019_animal_diversity, ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_5243_2019_plant_diversity]. In Bolivia four of the payment-like initiatives showed marked environmental protection effects [ev_biodiversity_outcome_robertson05_1]. Community management retained forest cover in Nepal, India and Bolivia [ev_landscape_forest_cover_iufro20_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_3], and environmental condition improved in 56% of community-forest cases worldwide [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1].
conditionality: Two units found no gain: management transfers in Madagascar remained superficial and did not stop clearing [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2]. In the global community-forest review condition decreased in 32% of cases [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1], and in Bolivia two initiatives had intermediate and three weak protection effects [ev_biodiversity_outcome_robertson05_1]. The only measured species count is the Senegal study, which compares exclosures of different ages rather than closed with open land [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1]. The rest are compiler ratings, a qualitative report from a bundled watershed programme [ev_biodiversity_outcome_woldearegay17_2], a rapid qualitative rating of payment schemes, and forest-cover change standing in for biodiversity.

effect_mechanism: Both directions are reported. On the gain side, planted stands create habitat and attract seed dispersers: beneath framework-species plantings in northern Thailand thirty-six tree seedling species recruited naturally, 25 of them animal-dispersed [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wydhayagarn09_1], and the WOCAT compiler for dune afforestation in Turkmenistan rates habitat diversity as raised, noting that the vegetation on the barkhan sands now provides habitat for 25-27 species of plants and animals [ev_biodiversity_outcome_wocat_1529_2012_habitat_diversity]. A meta-analysis across 221 study landscapes found forest restoration enhances biodiversity by 15–84% and vegetation structure by 36–77% compared with degraded ecosystems [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles16_1], and a meta-analysis of terrestrial restoration found restored sites had 20% higher mean biodiversity than unrestored sites [ev_biodiversity_outcome_atkinson22_1]. effect_mechanism: Natural regeneration rebuilds biodiversity strongly as secondary forest develops. Across tropical chronosequences species richness recovers fastest and composition slowest, with richness after 20 years at 78% of old-growth values [ev_biodiversity_outcome_poorter21_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_poorter21_2]; tree species richness in Brazil's Atlantic Forest rises with time since disturbance [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_1]; and in the western Andes of Colombia restored bird and dung beetle communities closely resembled those of old growth forests after 15–30 yr [ev_biodiversity_outcome_chazdon16_1]. A pantropical meta-analysis finds natural regeneration outperforms active planting for plants, birds and invertebrates [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles17_1], and in Senegal's southern Groundnut Basin woody species richness in exclosures rose from 27 species after 1 year to 51 species after 5 and 12 years, an increase of more than 52% [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1].
conditionality: Recovery of composition and endemism is slow: composition after 20 years was only 33% of old-growth values [ev_biodiversity_outcome_poorter21_1], and in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest regaining mature-forest endemism was estimated to take 1987 years [ev_biodiversity_outcome_liebsch08_3]. A global meta-analysis found biodiversity in naturally regenerated forests lower than in reference forests for every class of socioeconomic, biogeographic and ecological factor it examined [ev_biodiversity_outcome_latawiec16_1]; that comparison is with old-growth or less-disturbed forest, not with the degraded land regeneration starts from, so it is held out of the class as a recovery shortfall, not a loss caused by regeneration. The pantropical meta-analysis compares regeneration with planting rather than with degraded land [ev_biodiversity_outcome_crouzeilles17_1], and the Senegal result compares exclosures of different ages at one site rather than exclosures with open grazed land [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badji13_1]. The gain accrues to the regenerating forest and the landscape, not to the adopting farmer's fields.

effect_mechanism: The findings that set the rating point toward a small biodiversity loss, but none states how large it is. A review of nature-based solutions states that if non-native tree plantations replace intact native ecosystems such as ancient grasslands, peatlands or woodlands, the outcomes for biodiversity will be poor [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_1]. On the Orissa coast of India, extensive Casuarina plantations established as a storm protection measure caused destruction to olive ridley sea turtle nesting beaches [ev_biodiversity_outcome_badola05_12]. A review of coastal tree belts reports, partly from earlier work, that in India sand dunes have been flattened to make way for Casuarina plantations, destroying sea turtle nesting habitat, that Casuarina roots can prevent turtles from nesting above the high tide line, and that Casuarina is known to harm tropical birds and invade mangroves [ev_biodiversity_outcome_feagin10_2]. A review of coastal tree belts in Vietnam argues that plantings of non-native species may damage native ecosystems, noting, second-hand, that Casuarina tends to invade mangrove forests in low-salinity settings [ev_biodiversity_outcome_veettil21_2]. The nature-based solutions review also reports research in north-west India showing that although afforestation activities can lead to an aggregate increase in forest cover, in most cases they result in loss of diversity and promote monocultures [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_4]. Against this, the review allows a gain in a narrower case: establishing plantations of non-native trees in a highly degraded landscape might benefit biodiversity locally if the trees enable native vegetation to regenerate, or regionally if plantations take pressure off native biodiverse forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_2]. An INRAE expert synthesis's own small meta-analysis of species richness in plantations against natural regeneration of the stand after regeneration cutting finds no clear difference: -0.24, a very imprecise estimate from a very small number of cases, with an interval that spans zero [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_1]. Cited Canadian studies compared plantations with forest left to regrow after clear-cutting: spruce plantations had less rich and less diverse moss communities [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_5], while hybrid larch plantations had significantly richer plant communities and hybrid poplar plantations showed no clear difference [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_4].
conditionality: The loss is stated without a size: the loss-side units are review statements and a cited case, none of which measures the decline against the land a plantation replaced, so the row reports a direction only. What separates loss from gain is what the plantation replaces: intact native ecosystems, a nesting beach or a diverse cover replaced by monocultures on the loss side [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_1, ev_biodiversity_outcome_badola05_12, ev_biodiversity_outcome_feagin10_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_4], a highly degraded landscape where the trees help native vegetation return on the gain side [ev_biodiversity_outcome_seddon21_2]. Both coastal reviews are second-hand for most of their harm statements, and the Vietnam review hedges its warning as something that may happen [ev_biodiversity_outcome_feagin10_2, ev_biodiversity_outcome_veettil21_2]. The pooled comparison against regeneration is not significant [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_1], and the Canadian results differ by tree species and by group of plants, and are second-hand [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_4, ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_5]. Three further units point toward loss but are held out of the class because they compare plantations with reference native forest rather than with the starting point of a project: a global meta-analysis found tree plantations supported on average 29.3% lower species-specific abundance than reference native forests (95% interval 22.0 to 35.9%) [ev_biodiversity_outcome_hua22_1], INRAE states that plantations generally lead to decreases in biodiversity, or at least to changes in composition at the expense of native species [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_6], and it cites a 40% loss of local species richness in forest plantations relative to uncut control forest [ev_biodiversity_outcome_inrae23_2]. These describe a shortfall from a natural baseline, not a restoration effect. The INRAE evidence is temperate and boreal, and only the Indian cases come from the low- and lower-middle-income target. effect_mechanism: Restoring forest cover rebuilds the carbon stored in trees and soil that cleared or degraded land lacks. A global meta-analysis puts natural regeneration removal rates at 9.1–18.8 t CO2 per hectare per year during the first 20 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_3]. A pantropical synthesis of field plots gives above-ground biomass growth in naturally regrowing secondary forest, for example 7.6 tonnes of dry matter per hectare per year in younger African rainforest stands and 0.5 in older subtropical Asian mountain stands [ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_22]. A global model puts the average rate of natural forest regrowth at 3.16 Mg C per hectare per year [ev_carbon_sequestration_cookpatton20_2]. Planting native trees on former pasture in Brazil built up 21.85, 25.78 and 38.29 Mg/ha of carbon in successively older plantings [ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_3]. Protection and community forest management keep carbon in standing forest by retaining cover, measured as forest-cover change in payment schemes, community forests and GEF sites [ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_1]. A global model of natural climate solutions finds reforestation is the largest natural pathway, with a maximum mitigation potential, under food, fibre and biodiversity safeguards, of 2.7–17.9 Pg CO2e per year (95% confidence interval) [ev_carbon_sequestration_griscom17_1].
conditionality: The gain is moderate rather than large, and much of the size evidence is not a fresh measurement. The IPCC values are compiled default tables carried forward from earlier guidance with a stated uncertainty of plus or minus 90% and no sample size [ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc19_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_ipcc19_4], the global regrowth rates are model outputs for above-ground carbon [ev_carbon_sequestration_cookpatton20_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_cookpatton20_2], the plot synthesis and IPCC tables report dry matter, not carbon, and the global reforestation figure is a model of total potential across the world, not a per-hectare rate, with a wide range that its authors call highly uncertain [ev_carbon_sequestration_griscom17_1]. One source names a harm: afforestation on peaty soils can lead to losses of soil carbon that outweigh that sequestered as the trees grow [ev_carbon_sequestration_seddon21_7], so organic and peat soils need separate treatment. Four units found no gain: soil carbon under forest did not increase significantly over cropland in the first 0–5 years [ev_soil_organic_carbon_yang23_5], a REDD+ pilot in Nepal had no significant effect on forest carbon in community forests [ev_carbon_sequestration_snilstveit19_1], and in Madagascar transfer of management to communities remained superficial while clearing continued [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2]. Forest cover and soil carbon enter as parts of the carbon picture, not direct measures of it, and practitioner ratings make up several of the agreeing units.

A global meta-analysis gives natural regeneration removal rates of 9.1–18.8 t CO2 per hectare per year during the first 20 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_bernal18_3]. A pantropical synthesis of field plots gives above-ground biomass growth of up to 7.6 tonnes of dry matter per hectare per year in younger African rainforest stands, falling to 0.5 in older subtropical Asian mountain stands [ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_1, ev_carbon_sequestration_requena19_22]. Field chronosequences agree: Amazon secondary forests held 50% (229 t/ha) of mature forest biomass after 25 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_gehring05_1], Colombian Andean regrowth reached about half of old-growth carbon within 15–30 years [ev_carbon_sequestration_chazdon16_1], and an Atlantic Forest fragment regrown for 60 years reached 297 Mg/ha against 313 Mg/ha in preserved forest nearby [ev_carbon_sequestration_azevedo18_5]. conditionality: Above-ground biomass recovers slowly, taking 12 decades by one pantropical estimate [ev_carbon_sequestration_poorter21_1], so a project cycle captures only the early part of the gain. Much of the size evidence is modelled: the global regrowth rates are model outputs for above-ground carbon, assume steady growth over 30 years, and the soil rate of 0.42 Mg C per hectare per year is a default its authors say needs further research [ev_carbon_sequestration_cookpatton20_1, ev_soil_organic_carbon_cookpatton20_3]; the global potential holds only if regrowing forests can establish and persist [ev_carbon_sequestration_williams24_1]. The field chronosequences are from upper-middle-income Brazil and Colombia. Young regrowth holding less than old-growth is incomplete recovery, not a loss.

effect_mechanism: Protecting and managing forest keeps carbon stored in standing biomass and lets more build up. GEF sustainable forest management sites sequester more carbon each year than their counterfactual and avoid deforestation [ev_carbon_sequestration_gefieo19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_2], community forest management reduced deforestation in Nepal and increased forest cover in Puebla, Mexico [ev_landscape_forest_cover_iufro20_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1], environmental condition improved after community forest management in 56% of the 524 cases tracking it in a global analysis [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1], and the India compiler states that carbon storage is increased by the plantation, citing an average sequestration rate of 3.5 t ha -1 yr-1 for Van Panchayat forests [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_5243_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. A meta-analysis of payments for environmental services found improved forest cover (SMD = 0.32, 95% CI [0.10, 0.55]) and reduced deforestation against comparison areas [ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_snilstveit19_2]; Van Panchayats in India improved the annual forest cover change rate by 0.40 percentage points and municipal management in Bolivia by 0.80 [ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_samii14_3]; protected areas retained more forest than comparable unprotected land (Hedges' g of 0.17) [ev_landscape_forest_cover_malh25_2]; and World Bank evaluations report reduced deforestation under participatory forest management [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_2, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ieg13_1]. A global model finds existing secondary forests kept standing could remove 20.7 MgC per hectare on average over their best 25-year window, against 18.8 for new regeneration [ev_carbon_sequestration_robinson25_2], and that 8-year-old forest in the Brazilian Amazon would remove 36% more carbon by 2030 than newly growing stands (10.5 versus 7.7 MgC per hectare) [ev_carbon_sequestration_robinson25_3]. A global model of natural climate solutions finds that avoiding the conversion of existing forest offers the second largest maximum and cost-effective mitigation potential, with relatively low uncertainty (±17%) [ev_carbon_sequestration_griscom17_10].
conditionality: The class is held at moderate because the only size estimates for carbon come from models: the forest-keeping comparison is a model of above-ground carbon in existing secondary forest, not measured removals [ev_carbon_sequestration_robinson25_2, ev_carbon_sequestration_robinson25_3], the GEF carbon estimate is also derived from a model over existing forest [ev_carbon_sequestration_gefieo19_1], and the global avoided-conversion pathway is a model that states its size only in a figure, adding that costs may matter less than public policy challenges where land tenure is unclear [ev_carbon_sequestration_griscom17_10]. Much of the rest is forest-cover change standing in for carbon, and the India figure is a compiler's citation of earlier work [ev_carbon_sequestration_wocat_5243_2019_emission_of_carbon_and_greenhouse_gases]. Several units found no effect: community management transfers in Madagascar did not halt clearing [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_ramamo12_2], the REDD+ pilot in Nepal had an insignificant effect on forest carbon in community forests (SMD = 0.09) [ev_carbon_sequestration_snilstveit19_1], and a boundary comparison of crown cover under Van Panchayats found no significant difference from neighbouring state forest [ev_landscape_forest_cover_somanathan09_1, ev_landscape_forest_cover_somanathan09_2], though a matched whole-sample comparison found pine crown cover higher under council management [ev_landscape_forest_cover_somanathan09_3]. Some GEF sites showed harmful outcomes [ev_landscape_forest_cover_gefieo19_3], condition decreased in 32% of community-forest cases in the global analysis [ev_landscape_forest_cover_hajjar21_1], the Mexican result has no counterfactual [ev_landscape_forest_cover_ceballos21_1], and the protected-area pool varies widely across contexts (I-squared of 96 percent) [ev_landscape_forest_cover_malh25_2]. All of this evidence is about existing forest, not restored forest, and the Nepal, Indian and Bolivian estimates are cited in systematic reviews.

effect_mechanism: The evidence on whether forest restoration gives a catchment more or less water is conflicting, because it splits by the kind of forest. Planted forest (plantations and afforestation) reduces the water leaving a catchment: a global systematic review (Filoso et al.) found that in about 80% of study cases annual water yield fell as forest cover expanded, with baseflow falling in 63% and groundwater in 67% of cases that measured them [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_1, ev_water_regulation_filoso17_2, ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_filoso17_1]; a review of trees and water (Ellison et al.) restates the catchment syntheses, including Farley et al. 2005, as showing substantial losses in streamflow after afforestation and reforestation [ev_water_yield_ellison17_1]; and older tropical reviews (Bruijnzeel; Hamilton) report declines after planting pines or eucalypts on degraded grass- or cropland, with low flows usually diminished as well, especially where fast-growing, heavy water-using species are used [ev_water_yield_bruij90_3, ev_water_yield_ham08_6]. Fenced-off natural regrowth in a poorer country points the other way: a meta-analysis from Ethiopia (Meaza et al.) found the baseflow from catchments with exclosures was 1.5 to 4 times greater than from cropland [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1]. The plantation family's own row, built on Farley et al. 2005, adds that dry-season flows fall proportionally more than annual flows after planting, especially in dry regions.
conditionality: What separates the two sides is the forest planted and the place. The losses come mostly from fast-growing exotic plantations on former grassland or cropland, and Filoso's cases are dominated by temperate and Oceania studies that pool restoration with forestry and afforestation [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_1, ev_water_yield_bruij90_3]. Trees use more water than the grass or crops they replace, through rain caught and evaporated from the canopy in wet spells and higher transpiration in dry periods [ev_water_yield_bruij90_3]; in water-limited places large-scale afforestation will worsen water scarcity, a management statement (Zhang et al.) citing an earlier source [ev_water_yield_zhang17_7]. The gains come from exclosures on degraded Ethiopian land compared with cropland [ev_water_regulation_meaza22_1], from model runs of large-scale reforestation in China and Myanmar (Teo et al.) that raised water yield in some regions by 11.4% to 84.9% while others saw small, non-significant falls [ev_water_regulation_teo22_1, ev_water_regulation_teo22_4, ev_water_regulation_teo22_5], from a modelled spruce reforestation in China retold by a review [ev_water_yield_zhang17_6], and from long-term records at two logged temperate US forests where the authors say succession may explain higher summer streamflow [ev_water_yield_jon12_3]. Zhang et al. found no significant link between forest gain and annual runoff in small watersheds, a significant fall only in large ones, and some watersheds where runoff rose [ev_water_yield_zhang17_2, ev_water_yield_zhang17_3, ev_water_yield_zhang17_5]. Natural regrowth after logging also reduces stream yield back toward pre-cutting levels as the forest regrows [ev_water_yield_ham87_3, ev_water_yield_bruij90_4], so regrowth is not always a gain. Much of the evidence is second-hand, modelled or from high-income or unspecified settings; the one measured gain in a low-income country is the Ethiopian exclosure synthesis. For an investment, the type of forest and the dryness of the site decide which side applies.

effect_mechanism: A global systematic review pooling forest restoration with forestry and afforestation found that annual water yield decreased in about 80% of study cases reporting it and increased in 6% [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_1], baseflow decreased in 63% of cases [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_2], groundwater levels or recharge decreased in 67% of the studies reporting them [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_filoso17_1], and no water-yield gains were observed in the meta-analysed subset [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_3]. A global review of forest change found a significant negative relationship between forest cover gain and annual runoff in large watersheds [ev_water_yield_zhang17_3], and another review states that evidence typically highlights substantial losses in streamflow following afforestation and reforestation [ev_water_yield_ellison17_1]. Tropical forest canopies commonly intercept up to 35 per cent of rainfall, which evaporates without reaching soil water reserves, and much of the water that does soak in is used by the trees themselves [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1].
conditionality: This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks how much water leaves the catchment, not whether the restored land itself holds more, and a loss here can coexist with a local gain in the water stress rows [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_1]. The syntheses read scale differently: in the systematic review the decrease shrinks at larger time and space scales [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_3], while the global review found no significant relationship in small watersheds and a significant reduction only in large ones [ev_water_yield_zhang17_2, ev_water_yield_zhang17_3]. The same global review records a minority of watersheds where runoff increased with forest cover gain [ev_water_yield_zhang17_5]. The reviews pool restoration with other forest cover gain; the systematic review reports vote counts rather than sizes, is dominated by temperate and Oceania studies, and the baseflow cases are few [ev_water_regulation_filoso17_2]. effect_mechanism: Plantations strongly cut the water leaving a catchment, and they cut dry-season flow proportionally more than annual flow. A global synthesis of afforestation (Farley et al.) found annual runoff fell on average by 44% when grasslands and 31% when shrublands were planted [ev_water_yield_farley05_1, ev_water_yield_farley05_2]; low flow fell in the same way but by an even larger proportion, and the authors predict low-flow losses even more severe than annual losses, possibly turning streams in dry regions from flowing all year to flowing only part of the year [ev_water_yield_farley05_3, ev_water_yield_farley05_7]. Losses were far greater at the driest grassland site, 62%, which the authors read as afforestation hitting water yield harder in drier regions [ev_water_yield_farley05_4]; on former grassland, eucalypts cut runoff by 75% and pines by 40% [ev_water_yield_farley05_5, ev_water_yield_farley05_6]. In Fiji, planting Caribbean pine in dry-zone grasslands cut dry-season streamflow by 65 percent [ev_water_yield_ham08_7], and in South Africa, where nearly all plantations are on former native grassland, water reductions are in some cases felt as soon as two years after planting [ev_water_yield_ham08_10]. A national model for New Zealand (Dymond et al.) finds new pine forests reduce water yield by between 30% and 50% [ev_water_yield_dymond12_2], and a review (Seddon et al.) reports that China's Grain-for-Green programme used mainly fast-growing non-native species that have reduced water supply, and that intensively managed plantations may reduce water availability in arid regions [ev_water_yield_seddon21_10, ev_water_yield_seddon21_9].
conditionality: These are afforestation and production-plantation results, mostly paired catchments where grassland or shrubland was replaced by fast-growing pine or eucalypt. In proportional terms low flow kept falling as plantations aged to about 25 years and then began to recover somewhat [ev_water_yield_farley05_7]; in South Africa the largest decreases come early in fast-growing stands and then diminish [ev_water_yield_ham08_10]. The New Zealand figure is modelled, the Fiji and South Africa cases and the Grain-for-Green result are retold by reviews, and the settings are high-income or upper-middle-income; none is in a low-income country. Two units compare plantations with natural forest rather than with the land planted, so they are held out of the class: native-species plantations aged 25 to 45 years give dry-season streamflow deficits exceeding 50% relative to old-growth forest, a US finding cited second-hand [ev_water_regulation_iufro18_3], and a global meta-analysis (Hua et al.) found 13.4% lower water yield in tree plantations than in reference native forests [ev_water_yield_hua22_1]. effect_mechanism: Forests use more water than the land cover that replaces them, so standing forest passes less water downstream. As both natural and human-established forests use more water than most replacement land cover, even partial forest removal increases downstream water yields [ev_water_yield_ham08_1], and replacing forest cover with other land uses almost always results in increased runoff and streamflow [ev_water_yield_faocifor05_2]; a UNESCO review of moist tropical forest hydrology calls it beyond doubt that both natural and mature man-made forests use more water than most agricultural crops or grassland [ev_water_yield_bruij90_1]. A worldwide review of paired catchments found that forest cutting consistently gave more total water yield, in proportion to cutting intensity, because tall forests evaporate and transpire more; Hamilton retells it in both his earlier essay and his later FAO synthesis, so it counts once [ev_water_yield_ham87_1, ev_water_yield_ham08_4]. Reported first-year increases after forest clearance range between 110 and 825 mm, depending on local rainfall, and converting lowland rain forest to well managed grassland or annual cropping may produce permanent increases of 200 - 300 mm a year [ev_water_yield_bruij90_1, ev_water_yield_bruij90_2]. The extra flow arrives through the year: in most tropical small-basin experiments the bulk of the increase came in the dry season or baseflow [ev_water_yield_bruij90_15], the FAO synthesis puts the greatest percentage increase in the dry season, citing that review among others [ev_water_yield_ham08_2], and Hamilton's essay reports increased flows throughout the year, including the dry season [ev_water_yield_ham87_2]. Daily late-summer flows rose by up to 300% after experimental harvest, though most daily changes were 50% or less [ev_water_yield_jon12_2]. Global syntheses agree: more forest cover loss tends to increase annual runoff in both large and small watersheds [ev_water_yield_zhang17_1], an increase in forest coverage reduces the share of rainfall leaving as runoff [ev_water_yield_zhou15_1], and changes to forests in water-limited watersheds can lead to larger water-yield responses [ev_water_yield_zhou15_2]. Harvesting or removing forest also raises groundwater levels [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ham08_1].
conditionality: This row is for downstream users and basin planners: it asks how much water leaves the catchment, not whether the protected land itself holds more, and it can coexist with the local gains recorded in the protection water stress row. Every unit compares existing forest with its harvest, clearance or loss, which is why the row sits in the protection family and not in the forest restoration roll-up; none measures the outcome of a protection or community forest management project. Two results run the other way. Where infiltration after forest removal is degraded so far that extra stormflow exceeds the baseflow gain, diminished dry-season flow is the result [ev_water_yield_bruij90_16]; the dry-season gains above come from controlled experiments where infiltration was kept, so this is the case they leave out. Very small summer events also decreased by more than 40% in the first 2 years after canopy removal in the fog-prone Fox Creek basins [ev_water_yield_jon00_1]. Nulls stay named: 12 (of 61) large and 33 (of 252) small watersheds showed no significant change in annual runoff despite forest cover loss [ev_water_yield_zhang17_4], and basins of 7 to 727 km2 on Hainan and the 14500 km2 Pasak basin in northern Thailand showed no systematic streamflow change despite extensive forest loss; the review expects detectable change mainly where forest is replaced by annual cropping rather than left to regenerate [ev_water_yield_bruij90_9]. The groundwater statement also cuts both ways: removal can move soil salts into the rooting zone [ev_groundwater_recharge_potential_ham08_1].

effect_mechanism: Reforestation slows storm runoff and lowers flood peaks, mostly in catchment models and at local scale. Catchment models show it: in Slovakia's Hornad watershed a reforestation scenario cut a simulated flood peak from 84.8 to 74.9 m3/s and, for a 50% increase of forest, reduced peaks by about 24% on average in rain-duration tests, more for short storms than long ones [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_1, ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_3], and an afforestation simulation for Luxembourg's Alzette basin decreased the peak by 8% [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_5]. A systematic review of forest cover and catchment flooding finds peak flow changes by roughly half the change in forest cover, so a 20% increase in forest cover tends to reduce peak flow by 10% across small, medium and large catchments, with only minor differences in mean reductions across event intensities up to the 1% AEP event; the review attributes this to forests detaining floodwater through infiltration, canopy interception and evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_1, ev_flood_hazard_herath25_5]. Another systematic review found that flooding or peak flows decreased with forest cover expansion in 82% of the studies reporting them [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]. A UNESCO review of moist tropical forest hydrology states that the beneficial effects of reforesting, terracing and contouring degraded lands on stormflow and peakflow are evident at small-basin scale, as is the regenerative capacity of most ecosystems when left alone [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_6, ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_7]. In a US experimental basin the gradual recovery of peak discharges over time after clear-cutting, as vegetation regrew, is attributed to changes in evapotranspiration [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. An FAO synthesis accepts that locally, for frequent short, low-intensity storm events, flash flooding should be reduced where soils are deep [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_7], and a cited synthesis expects afforestation in energy-limited environments to help reduce flood risks [ev_flood_hazard_zhang17_1]. An Ethiopian WOCAT compiler for a regeneration-based technology rates downstream flooding as strongly reduced, noting that runoff from the watershed is highly reduced [ev_flood_hazard_wocat_1072_2011_downstream_flooding]. A global study of natural climate solutions also lists flood control among reforestation's well-demonstrated co-benefits, citing an earlier assessment, with no size given [ev_flood_hazard_griscom17_3].
conditionality: What separates the benefit from the nulls is scale and storm size. The gains are local, modelled or small-storm results; the nulls are about large basins and floods on the plains. The FAO synthesis finds no evidence that reforesting watersheds reduces or prevents floods except at the very local scale of a few hundred hectares [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_5, ev_flood_hazard_ham08_6]. A Himalayan analysis concludes that reforestation will not likely have significant beneficial impact on local flooding, and certainly not on the hydrological character of the Ganges and Brahmaputra mainstreams [ev_flood_hazard_ives87_1], and a conference overview warns that reforestation in the mountains conceived as a palliative for the problems of the plains is likely to reap only disappointment [ev_flood_hazard_ivesmt87_1], and both come from the same lead author, so they count as a single line of argument. An FAO–CIFOR review concludes that massive programmes of forestation proclaimed as the answer to preventing floods simply will not do the job, although reforestation may have many other benefits [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_3], and a published comment argues that reforestation does not necessarily reduce flooding, for example if soil properties do not recover, river bed morphology does not change, and settlements, roads and drains remain unaltered [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_5]. A review of coastal tree belts adds a coastal null: the science on short-period wave damping should not be taken to show that vegetation can reduce the effects of storm surges [ev_flood_hazard_feagin10_1]; this is an expert argument about coastal plantings, not a measurement. These are expert positions and reviews rather than new measurements. The co-benefit listing is second-hand and states no size, place or scale [ev_flood_hazard_griscom17_3]. The UNESCO review's statement is local only, its supporting table cannot be read so no size is available, and the planting half of the sentence pools reforesting with terracing and contouring, so it cannot be credited to trees alone [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_6, ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_7]. The flood-cover review adds that afforestation yields only gradual reductions, smaller than the rises in peak flow that follow deforestation and shaped by forest maturity, with peak flow in small catchments falling by up to 14% on limited data [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_2, ev_flood_hazard_herath25_4]; its pooled peak-flow points come from modelled scenarios in mostly temperate catchments, so it is a synthesis of other studies' models rather than new measurement. The modelled benefit itself shrinks as rain continues, from 29% for the shortest rain duration to 17% for the longest [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_3], and all catchment models are scenarios of large forest-cover gains in temperate high-income basins; the largest figure, a 42.3% peak reduction from converting all arable land to forest, is a secondary citation with no basin named [ev_flood_hazard_bahremand06_4]. The Oregon recovery comes from a clear-cut harvest study, measured against the freshly cut state rather than against unrestored land, and the paper does not say whether the regrowth was planted or natural [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_5]. The low- and lower-middle-income evidence is a compiler rating and expert positions, not measured flows or flood damage. The forest-water review pools restoration with forestry and afforestation and reports vote counts rather than magnitudes [ev_flood_hazard_filoso17_1]. No unit measures a benefit at severe or extreme flood; the only reading at the 1% AEP event is that review's pooled modelled points [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_5]. Studies of what existing forest does, such as harvest experiments and the Himalayan essays on forest loss, sit in the protection family row and do not set this class. For farmers the effect is off-site: any reduction arrives downstream of the restored land, not on their plots.

effect_mechanism: This row describes the flood regulation that standing forest provides and that protection keeps; nearly all of it is evidence about existing forest, read through what happens when it is cut. In paired experimental basins in Oregon, a high-income setting, discharges in small basins increased by 50% in the first 5 years after clear-cutting and were 25 to 40% higher than pretreatment up to 25 years later, and forest harvesting with roads has increased peak discharges by as much as 50% in small basins and 100% in large basins over the past 50 years [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_2, ev_flood_hazard_jg96_3, ev_flood_hazard_jg96_1]. A later analysis of the same basins found large events increased by 25% at Andrews 1, 16% at Andrews 6 and 26% at Coyote 3 after 100% clear-cutting [ev_flood_hazard_jon00_1]. The same Oregon study separates the event types. Forest canopy removal accounted for significant increases (31–116%) in peak discharges during the first postharvest decade in 8 of 10 treated basins, but the affected events were small and fell in the fall (September–November), when soils are in moisture deficit, rather than in spring [ev_water_regulation_jon00_1]. Changes in snowpack dynamics accounted for significant increases (25–31%) in winter rain-on-snow events in four of five basins at the H. J. Andrews Experimental Forest [ev_water_regulation_jon00_6]. Two reviews of forest hydrology state the general rule: after forest cutting or conversion there is usually, in response to each storm, an increase in peak flow, storm-flow volume and storm-flow duration [ev_flood_hazard_ham87_5], and a certain increase in stormflow volume and peakflow cannot be avoided after forest conversion, with the relative increase largest for small events (which may be doubled) and smallest for large ones (perhaps in the order of 10 per cent or less) [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_5]. An FAO synthesis states that partial or complete removal of tree cover accelerates water discharge, increasing the risk of flood during the rainy season, and that for frequent rainfall events of short duration or low intensity forested soils may reduce or prevent flash floods locally [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_1, ev_flood_hazard_ham08_3]. At the local scale forests and forest soils reduce runoff through enhanced infiltration and storage, and peak flows rise after forest removal in small experimental catchments [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_1, ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_2]. A country-level analysis of developing countries predicted that a further hypothetical 10% loss of natural forest cover would raise flood frequency by 3.5% to 28.1% and flood duration by 3.8% to 7.9% [ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_1, ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_2]; in Peninsular Malaysia, a river-basin panel study by Tan-Soo and colleagues found that converting 1% of a basin from inland forest to oil palm increased the number of days flooded by 26.8%, and to rubber by 26.5%, with conversion to urban use also having a large effect (semi-elasticity = 35.9%) [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_1, ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_2, ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_4]; a systematic review of forest cover and catchment flooding finds that deforestation consistently increases peak flows [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_3]; and in Swiss valleys with more than 30% forest, snowmelt was more gradual and flooding risk lower [ev_flood_hazard_iufro18_2].
conditionality: The class is moderate because the evidence agrees only in part. The harvest studies, the forest-loss analyses and the two classic reviews describe what existing forest does; they enter through the existing-forest comparator (the flood-cover review's deforestation reading among them [ev_flood_hazard_herath25_3]), which routes them to this protection family and keeps them out of the restoration families, so none of them is a restoration or protection-programme result. The Malaysian study also carries the harm finding in this row: where the forest converted was wetland (peat-swamp) forest, deforestation reduced flooding, a large effect (semi-elasticity = 38.0%), which the authors link to drainage installed at conversion lowering the water level; so keeping forest is not a flood defence in every forest type [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_3]. The same study found no significant effect of deforestation on the number of floods per month, which the authors put down to a problem in defining that variable rather than to forest having no effect [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_5]. Its inland-forest figures are semi-elasticities per 1% of basin area converted, not whole-catchment contrasts, and the oil palm and rubber results are from a single period of conversion, not restoration [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_1, ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_2], while the urban figure was not estimated very precisely (P = 0.094) [ev_flood_hazard_tansoo14_4]. The Oregon large-basin increase is bundled with forest road construction and is stated as an upper bound, as much as [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_1]. The service fades with storm size and basin size. Complete clear-cutting without roads produced significant increases in fall and winter events but not for large events as a group [ev_flood_hazard_jg96_4], and at Andrews 10 large events did not change after 100% clear-cutting [ev_flood_hazard_jon00_2]. In the same study other types of winter events did not change, so only rain-on-snow peaks rose in winter [ev_water_regulation_jon00_7], and in the fog-prone basins changes in cloud water interception apparently offset changes in evapotranspiration in two partially cut basins [ev_water_regulation_jon00_5]. The fall increases came in small events (0.22- or 0.28-year return periods), not in large events [ev_water_regulation_jon00_1]. For the rarer prolonged or high-intensity storms, once the soil layer becomes saturated water will run off even where there is full, undisturbed forest cover [ev_flood_hazard_ham08_4]; Hamilton's earlier essay makes the same point, that for major storms the effect of forest on or forest off is dwarfed by the rainfall itself, since soil can only store so much water [ev_flood_hazard_ham87_6]. He judges that the June 1985 floods that killed 237 persons in six Indian states were caused by too much rain in too short a time, with some areas receiving 414 mm in 24 hours on already saturated soils, and that even a fully forested basin would have flooded; this is his judgement, not data [ev_flood_hazard_ham87_12]. Forest soils reduce runoff only in small-scale rainfall events, which are not responsible for severe downstream flooding, and forests cannot stop catastrophic large-scale floods caused by severe meteorological events [ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_1, ev_flood_hazard_faocifor05_2]; and small to medium peak flows are affected most while the largest events do not change noticeably [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_3]. At basin scale the link is not shown. A worldwide review of watershed research found no cause and effect between forest cutting in the headwaters and floods in the lower basin; Hamilton cites it both in his earlier essay, where he adds that there are no valid reasons to suggest forests can prevent major floods on the large rivers of the subcontinent, and in his later FAO synthesis, so this is a single finding [ev_flood_hazard_ham87_4, ev_flood_hazard_ham08_2]. Long records from meso-scale basins of up to 14500 km2 in Taiwan and northern Thailand that had lost much forest showed no systematic trend in flood magnitude, climate dominating, although the review notes that much of that forest loss was probably followed by regeneration rather than cropping [ev_flood_hazard_bruij90_8]. A Himalayan analysis contends that on the Himalayan scale human influences, so far, are insignificant [ev_flood_hazard_ives87_2]. The cross-country analysis itself found little evidence that further forest loss changed flood deaths or damage [ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_3, ev_flood_hazard_bradshaw07_4], and a reanalysis found the correlation between forest cover or cover loss and flood frequency appears absent [ev_flood_hazard_vandijk09_1]. Every unit compares forest with cleared or less-forested land, so the row shows what losing forest costs rather than the outcome of a protection or community forestry programme. Benefits fall downstream, off-site for farmers.

effect_mechanism: Keeping forest standing supports diets and growth, though the gain from co-management itself is small. In a multi-country study of children in rural areas, Rasolofoson et al. find that high exposure to forests causes children to have at least 25% greater dietary diversity than no exposure, an average difference of 0.4 points (95% confidence interval 0.29 to 0.51) against matched non-forest households, and raises the share of households where children ate vitamin A– or iron-rich food by at least 11 and 16 percentage points [ev_food_security_rasolofoson18_1, ev_food_security_rasolofoson18_2, ev_food_security_rasolofoson18_3, ev_food_security_rasolofoson18_4]. A global forest and food-security assessment cites Ickowitz et al. (2014), who found children's dietary diversity rising with community tree cover across 21 African countries, and Johnson et al. (2013), who found that children in Malawi communities that experienced deforestation had less diverse diets [ev_food_security_iufro15_2, ev_food_security_iufro15_1]. Naidoo et al. find that living near multiple-use protected areas with documented tourism would increase children's height-for-age growth scores by 9.8% and reduce the likelihood of stunting by 13.4% [ev_food_security_naidoo19_1]. In India the WOCAT compiler for broadleaf plantations, assisted tree regeneration and fodder nurseries reports better village self-sufficiency from more and better fodder and more water [ev_food_security_wocat_5243_2019_food_security_selfsufficiency]. In Malawi, households taking part in forest co-management through village natural resource management committees had a 1.62% higher food consumption score than non-participants, with wild foods collected from the reserves as the pathway the authors describe [ev_food_security_kimwanga26_3].
conditionality: The slight class reflects the size of the measured co-management effect: in Malawi the food consumption gain for committee members was small, and it comes from a cross-sectional comparison of members with non-members [ev_food_security_kimwanga26_3]. The forest-diet effect depends on community wealth: Rasolofoson et al. find it significant and beneficial in poor communities, insignificant at community GDP between US$3 billion and 5 billion, and reversed above US$5 billion, where forest exposure goes with less diverse children's diets; this is the measured harm on the row [ev_food_security_rasolofoson18_5]. Protected-area gains depend on tourism: no early childhood growth gains were found near protected areas without documented tourism [ev_food_security_naidoo19_2]. Under Mexico's payments for environmental services, as cited in a systematic review, a food index showed a statistically insignificant 0.09 SMD effect [ev_food_security_snilstveit19_1]. Most units compare people living near existing forest or protected areas with people who do not; they show what standing forest provides, not what a protection or community-management project adds, and the tree-cover and deforestation findings are cited second-hand.

effect_mechanism: Standing forest keeps the land surface cooler than cleared land, and protection keeps that cooling; the benefit is small and its size for heat stress is not stated. Satellite and flux tower data show tropical forest surfaces significantly cooler than nearby cleared areas, by 0.2–2.4 degrees C a year (mean 0.96) [ev_microclimate_buffering_lawrence22_1], and temperate forest cover cools by 0.02–1.0 degrees C (mean 0.4) [ev_microclimate_buffering_lawrence22_2]. A worldwide satellite comparison finds tropical forests 2.41 degrees C cooler than nearby open land over the day, and mid-latitude forests 0.27 degrees C cooler in the northern hemisphere and 0.97 in the southern [ev_microclimate_buffering_li15_1, ev_microclimate_buffering_li15_2]. In the tropics, places that lost forest between 2003 and 2018 saw afternoon temperatures in the hottest months rise by 1.6, 1.2 and 0.55 degrees C in the Americas, Africa and Asia, against 0.2, 0.4 and -0.01 where forest was kept [ev_microclimate_buffering_parsons21_1], and the time each day that is unsafe for heavy outdoor work rose by 0.33, 0.13 and 0.16 hours [ev_heat_stress_hazard_parsons21_1]. Deforestation led to warming of 0.38 degrees C in tropical and 0.16 in temperate regions [ev_microclimate_buffering_prevedello19_5]. In an Indonesian village survey, the most common reason villagers gave for why forests matter to health was that forests keep the environment cool [ev_microclimate_buffering_wolff18_1], and a cited Sumatran study found primary and secondary forests more than 4 degrees C cooler than nearby young oil palm plantations [ev_microclimate_buffering_wolff18_2]. Trees can keep cooling through long heatwaves thanks to deeper roots [ev_microclimate_buffering_ellison17_1], and a review reports that extremely hot days are significantly more common following deforestation [ev_microclimate_buffering_lawrence22_3], that historical deforestation explains about a third of the increase in the intensity of the hottest days [ev_microclimate_buffering_lawrence22_4], and that it has made hot dry summers two to four fold more frequent and intense [ev_microclimate_buffering_lawrence22_5].

In mid latitudes daytime cooling is largely offset by night warming [ev_microclimate_buffering_li15_2]. Every unit describes existing forest compared with open or cleared land; none evaluates a protection or community forestry project, and none measures restored forest. The Indonesian villager answers are perceptions, not measurements [ev_microclimate_buffering_wolff18_1], and the Sumatran figure is cited second-hand [ev_microclimate_buffering_wolff18_2]. The outdoor-work figures come from a model of what clearing forest costs, against places that kept forest [ev_heat_stress_hazard_parsons21_1]. Most of the evidence is land surface temperature, which is more sensitive than the temperature of the air at 2 m [ev_microclimate_buffering_lawrence22_2], not heat stress on crops, livestock or people, so the strength of the effect on heat stress is not stated. The heat-extreme findings are a review reporting other studies, two of them from model-based attribution [ev_microclimate_buffering_lawrence22_4, ev_microclimate_buffering_lawrence22_5].

effect_mechanism: In low- and lower-middle-income settings, closing degraded land to grazing and letting vegetation recover strongly lifts production on nearby farms. In Tigray, Ethiopia, households downstream of exclosures achieved notably higher crop yields than those next to open grazing areas in the 2023 season, by 188 to 222 kg/ha, and a panel estimate controlling for soil fertility, labour and fertilizer put the grain advantage at 586.6 kg/ha [ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_1, ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_2]. The advantage was greater in the first, drier year [ev_crop_yield_mezgebo26_3]. WOCAT compilers add the pathways: an Ethiopian area closure raised crop production because soil depth increased and soil fertility improved [ev_crop_yield_wocat_1072_2011_crop_production], and Tanzanian enclosures raised crop production through mulching materials, fodder through area enclosure and decline of forest fire, and animal production through nutritious cut and carry pastures [ev_crop_yield_wocat_1607_2014_crop_production, ev_forage_productivity_wocat_1607_2014_fodder_production, ev_livestock_productivity_wocat_1607_2014_animal_production].
conditionality: The measured evidence is a single Ethiopian study, and its gain is on cropland downstream of the exclosures compared with farms beside open grazing, not production on the closed land itself. On the gain side, farm output rose alongside restoration: under Brazil's Reflorestar payments programme, agricultural value added in the poorest-quartile municipalities rose by 8% and the value of agricultural production by approximately 14% [ev_agricultural_production_value_seixas24_2, ev_agricultural_production_value_seixas24_3], and on Turkmen barkhan sands the compiler rates fodder production as strongly increased because the planted sand-fixing species are also used as forage [ev_forage_productivity_wocat_1529_2012_fodder_production]. On the loss side, a meta-analysis of vegetation restoration in erosion zones found that returning cropland or bare land to forest left soil total nitrogen content not significantly changed overall (3.04%), and that it decreased by 16.84% in hot regions (MAT > 15 °C) and by 19.85% in humid regions (MAP > 800 mm) compared with cropland; the authors attribute this to higher plant uptake of soil nitrogen under high temperature and rainfall [ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_4, ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_6, ev_soil_nitrogen_yang23_7].

effect_mechanism: Forest restoration reduces rural poverty mainly by creating new or additional income: forestry wages, non-timber forest products, payments for environmental services, and labour tied to restoration programmes. effect_mechanism: Timber and protective plantations moderately raise household income in this evidence. In Vietnam a World Bank evaluation found the economic rate of return for smallholder plantations was 13.2% at completion, against 17.0% expected at appraisal [ev_economic_return_ieg18_1], and the financial gains for participating smallholders were substantial, mainly because low-interest loans from the project reduced up-front costs to near zero [ev_household_income_ieg18_1]. In Costa Rica, payments for environmental services on reforested land made up 18.66% of participants' income during the contract [ev_household_income_padilla17_1], other Latin American studies cited there found payments reach around 10% of family income [ev_household_income_padilla17_2], and participants' perceived economic benefit scored 63.9% of the maximum, mainly from covering planting and upkeep costs, family employment and secure land title [ev_household_income_padilla17_3]. A global cost analysis finds plantations would be profitable even without carbon payments across 28.3% of the area where they are feasible [ev_economic_return_busch24_1]. In Andhra Pradesh, India, a review reports, from the project's own material, returns from Casuarina coastal plantations of Rs. 25,000/ha (USD 600/ha) after 4 years, shared half with the community and half reinvested in more planting, plus access to fuelwood and small timber [ev_household_income_feagin10_3].
conditionality: No source measures a change in poverty itself: the evidence is rates of return, profitability and income shares. The Vietnamese gains depended on subsidised loans [ev_household_income_ieg18_1], the Costa Rican income comes from the payments rather than the timber, and the 63.9% figure is a perception score [ev_household_income_padilla17_1, ev_household_income_padilla17_3]. The global profitability figure is a model and says nothing about who benefits [ev_economic_return_busch24_1]. The Indian figure is second-hand from the project's own reporting, and the review notes that cutting trees for fuelwood works against the plantations' protective purpose [ev_household_income_feagin10_3]. Only the Indian case is from a lower-middle-income country; Costa Rica and Vietnam are upper-middle-income.

effect_mechanism: Protection and community forest management moderately reduce poverty through forest income and employment. Community forest management in Nepal reduced both poverty and deforestation across 18,000 community forests [ev_rural_poverty_iufro20_2], 68% of community forestry cases reporting livelihood outcomes showed income increases [ev_household_income_hajjar21_1], and community forestry in Madagascar had a small but beneficial impact on living standards [ev_household_income_iufro20_2]. Protected areas contributed to poverty alleviation in Costa Rica and Thailand [ev_rural_poverty_puri16_1, ev_rural_poverty_iufro20_1]; a meta-analysis of counterfactual studies finds small gains in local monetary outcomes (g = 0.028) and poverty outcomes (g = 0.117) [ev_household_income_kandel22_1, ev_rural_poverty_kandel22_1]; households in the Chitwan National Park buffer zone of Nepal have 19 percent higher per capita income [ev_household_income_kandel22_2]; and living within 10 km of protected areas with tourism lowers the likelihood of poverty by 16.1%, with poverty 8.8% lower near multiple-use protected areas [ev_rural_poverty_naidoo19_1, ev_rural_poverty_naidoo19_2]. Co-management raised regular forest income in Malawi by 26 per cent and by 66% for low-income households, consumption in Ethiopian participatory forest management communities by 35 per cent, and forest income near Uganda's National Forestry Authority forests by 16 per cent [ev_household_income_samii14_1, ev_household_income_samii14_2, ev_household_income_samii14_3, ev_household_income_samii14_6]. Around Malawi's forest reserves, taking part in co-management is associated with 17.48% more forestry income and 21.07% more non-forest income [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_1, ev_household_income_kimwanga26_2], 26.6% higher per capita income among the poorest households without rainfall shocks [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_6], and, after shocks, 57% higher forestry income [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_4] and a 31.4% per capita income gain for moderately poor households [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_7]; participants also owned more durable goods [ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_9, ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_10, ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_8, ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_12, ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_13]. World Bank support raised participating household incomes in Albania by an estimated 30 percent and in Honduras by 62 percent, and in Andhra Pradesh poorer households compensated for lost land access gained 40 percent [ev_household_income_ieg13_2, ev_household_income_ieg13_3, ev_household_income_ieg13_4]. Community forestry in Mexico's Sierra Norte de Puebla provides year-round wage labour and a profit share of 10 to 20 thousand pesos per member [ev_household_income_ceballos21_1], households near GEF sites in Uganda show income gains [ev_household_income_gefieo19_1], groups selling environmental services in Bolivia improved economically [ev_household_income_robertson05_1], and non-timber income rose after benefit-sharing at Bach Ma, Vietnam [ev_household_income_ieg18_3].
conditionality: The pool is divided. The global community-forest review that reports income gains in 68% of cases also records 26% with no change and 6.3% with decreases [ev_household_income_hajjar21_1]. In south-west Madagascar community management contracts were not profitable and did not raise incomes [ev_economic_return_ramamo12_1, ev_household_income_ramamo12_1]; the GEF forest-management portfolio has a benefit-cost ratio of 0.69 [ev_economic_return_gefieo19_1]; REDD+ contributions in Nepal were nominal, from 3.2% of the poorest households' income to 0.3% for the less poor, local studies found no effect of REDD+ on material well-being, and an analysis in Indonesia found potentially harmful effects [ev_household_income_iufro20_4, ev_household_income_iufro20_5, ev_household_income_iufro20_6]; payment programmes have a small beneficial or neutral effect on poverty [ev_rural_poverty_iufro20_3]; and Mexico's payment scheme was less cost-effective than a protected area [ev_economic_return_snilstveit19_2]. Benefits skew to the better-off: in Nepal poor and low-caste households receive much less while bearing more costs [ev_household_income_iufro20_3]; near Uganda's District Forestry Service forests forest income rose by an insignificant 2 per cent and lowest-quartile households lost 6 per cent and 10 per cent [ev_household_income_samii14_4, ev_household_income_samii14_5]; at Bach Ma benefits were shared unevenly and products over-harvested [ev_household_income_ieg18_3]. After rainfall shocks, Malawi participants held fewer durable assets than non-participants around Mua-Livulezi, a 2.846 unit decrease, and Vwaza Marsh, a 1.677 decrease [ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_11, ev_farm_asset_index_kimwanga26_14], participation did not stop shocks eroding non-forestry income by 36% [ev_household_income_kimwanga26_5], and the study compares members with non-members at a single point in time rather than before and after. Just two out of 37 closed World Bank protected-area projects achieved their livelihood aims, and benefit-sharing around Vietnam's special-use forests, averaging US$1,053 per community, was too small to have any discernible impact [ev_household_income_ieg13_1, ev_household_income_ieg18_2]. A large household survey adds that forests are a weak safety net: only 7.8% of households turned to forests as their main response to an income shock, 10.4% to any wild resource [ev_household_income_wunder14_1]; that unit is carried but does not set the class. The protected-area studies measure what living near standing forest provides, not a restoration outcome; the Colombian benefit of $411–1,236 per hectare a year is a carbon valuation, not cash income [ev_economic_return_wri17_3]; and many figures are review citations or World Bank estimates without a comparison group.

effect_mechanism: Tree cover reduces erosion by protecting the soil surface, slowing runoff and holding slopes, and the sub-practice rows agree on that direction. A UNESCO review of moist tropical forest hydrology locates the surface protection in the litter and herb layer: erosion is minimal where the soil surface is protected by a well-developed litter and herb layer, rises only slightly when the understorey is removed, and rises dramatically when the litter layer is destroyed or removed [ev_erosion_hazard_bruij90_10]. The same review states that tree planting, like soil conservation measures, may well reduce the sediment from surface erosion and shallow land slips entering the drainage system [ev_sediment_retention_bruij90_13]. In the passive regeneration evidence, an Ethiopian meta-analysis finds areas closed for grazing and agriculture had runoff coefficients of 4% against 19% on control sites [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_1], the Tanzanian enclosure compiler rates surface runoff as decreased as a result of vegetation cover and downstream siltation as decreased through improved vegetation cover and controlled erosion [ev_runoff_reduction_wocat_1607_2014_surface_runoff, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_1607_2014_downstream_siltation], and the higher probability of landslides after timber removal diminishes substantially 15–25 yr after harvesting as replacement trees mature [ev_erosion_hazard_sidle06_2]. The planting evidence carries the measured magnitudes: in Pakistan a watershed restoration reduced storm runoff and sediment yields by 55 and 78% [ev_runoff_reduction_hanif90_1, ev_erosion_hazard_hanif90_1], Chir pine planting with elimination of grazing at Balakot reduced surface runoff by 57% and sediment production by 69% against adjacent grazed land [ev_runoff_reduction_hanif90_2], tree planting on degraded Ethiopian catchments cut annual runoff from 242 to 148 mm/year [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_2], and vegetation restoration in China could reduce soil erosion by at least 80% once cover exceeds 60% [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_1]. A Slovak catchment model shows reforestation decreasing surface runoff [ev_runoff_reduction_bahremand06_1]. A meta-analysis of vegetation restoration in erosion zones finds that both forestland and grassland restoration of cropland or bare land were effective methods for controlling erosion, cutting sediment and runoff, with canopies, root systems and the organic surface layer not differing in their impact [ev_erosion_hazard_yang23_1, ev_runoff_reduction_yang23_2]. In Tigray, Ethiopia, upstream treatment with deep trenches, percolation pits and afforestation reduced siltation of May Demu dam by up to 60%, a figure the chapter takes from Woldearegay's earlier 2011 report, and in the Abreha Weatsbeha watershed the authors observed significant improvements in reducing soil erosion after afforestation, area closures and water-harvesting works [ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_3, ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_1]. FAO syntheses call forest restoration one of the best ways of reducing sedimentation in degraded cleared land, list reducing soil loss among the very good reasons for rehabilitating watersheds, and cite Taiwan, where a rehabilitation programme reduced reservoir sedimentation by 55 percent of the base rate [ev_sediment_retention_ham08_1, ev_erosion_hazard_ham08_1, ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. An FAO review of forests and landslides in Asia asserts that tree planting on susceptible slopes can reduce risk [ev_erosion_hazard_forbes11_1], and land abandonment with an increase in forest and grassland led to less soil erosion in one cited case [ev_erosion_hazard_iufro18_5]. At community-managed sites the India compiler credits trees and other vegetation with mitigating displacement of soil from upstream areas to the lowlands and with slowing sediment and runoff [ev_erosion_hazard_wocat_5243_2019_soil_loss, ev_sediment_retention_wocat_5243_2019_downstream_siltation], and a World Bank evaluation lists reduced soil erosion among the outcomes participatory forest management projects reported where they were monitored [ev_erosion_hazard_ieg13_1].
conditionality: The benefit is largely off-site for farmers: much of it is reduced runoff and sediment reaching downstream land and channels rather than better soil on their own plots [ev_sediment_retention_wocat_5243_2019_downstream_siltation]. Scale and time limit the downstream effect. The UNESCO review warns that, because of storage effects, it may take several decades for basins larger than several hundred square kilometres before stream sediment loads downstream become noticeably smaller [ev_sediment_retention_bruij90_14]. Nulls and dissent stay named. In China the soil conservation measures, including vegetation and engineering, contributed 12.1–13.9% sediment reduction in the Three-Gorge Reservoir Area, so the vegetation share should be less than 10% in most instances [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_2]; decreased Pearl River sediment loads had little to do with soil conservation measures [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_3]; and on the Loess Plateau an inversely decreasing trend of erosion reduction with vegetation cover was attributed to the immaturity of the planted species [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_4]. A Himalayan position paper judges that reforestation will not likely have significant beneficial impact on soil loss [ev_erosion_hazard_ives87_1], young second-growth timber falls far short of providing the root support of its older predecessors [ev_erosion_hazard_bishop64_5], abandoned land in previously terraced landscapes can be particularly prone to gully erosion and landslides [ev_erosion_hazard_iufro18_4], and the REDD+ pilot in Nepal had an insignificant effect on signs of soil erosion in community forests (SMD = −0.15, 95% CI [−0.31, 0.02]) [ev_erosion_hazard_snilstveit19_1]. The largest measured reductions are bundles: the Pakistan results combine planting with grazing control and, in the watershed study, erosion control structures, and the Taiwan programme combines reforestation with soil conservation on cultivated land, fire control and check dams, so none can be credited to tree cover alone [ev_erosion_hazard_hanif90_1, ev_sediment_retention_ham08_2]. The Tigray results are bundles of afforestation and area closures with trenches, percolation pits and check-dams, from showcase sites, and the dam figure is an upper bound carried from an earlier report [ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_3, ev_erosion_hazard_woldearegay17_1]. The UNESCO sediment statement also offers tree planting as one option among soil conservation measures, not as a measured tree effect [ev_sediment_retention_bruij90_13]. The erosion-zone meta-analysis reports its forest-only effect sizes only in a figure, so it sets the direction but not a size [ev_erosion_hazard_yang23_1]. The runoff results measure a component of erosion risk rather than soil loss [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_1]. Studies of what existing forest does, including logging and harvest landslide studies, sit in the protection family row and do not count here, and plantation results are kept in their own family row, out of this roll-up.

effect_mechanism: Planted cover reduces runoff and soil loss on the restored slope and catchment, so the benefit reaches farmers off-site, through less sediment and runoff arriving downslope and downstream rather than on the plot itself. In Pakistan a watershed restoration of tree planting, control of grazing and erosion control structures reduced storm runoff and sediment yields by 55 and 78% [ev_runoff_reduction_hanif90_1, ev_erosion_hazard_hanif90_1], and Chir pine planting with elimination of grazing at Balakot reduced surface runoff by 57% and sediment production by 69% against adjacent grazed areas with natural vegetation [ev_runoff_reduction_hanif90_2]. A review of Chinese vegetation restoration finds it could reduce soil erosion by at least 80% once vegetation cover exceeds 60% [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_1]. A Slovak catchment model shows reforestation decreasing surface runoff [ev_runoff_reduction_bahremand06_1], and in Ethiopia tree planting on degraded catchments reduced annual runoff depth from 242 to 148 mm/year [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_2]. A UNESCO review of moist tropical forest hydrology states that tree planting, like soil conservation measures, may well reduce the sediment from surface erosion and shallow land slips entering the drainage system [ev_sediment_retention_bruij90_13].
conditionality: The Pakistan results are bundles - planting with grazing control and, in the watershed study, check dams and spillways - so the reduction cannot be credited to planting alone [ev_erosion_hazard_hanif90_1, ev_runoff_reduction_hanif90_2]. The downstream effect is slow in large basins: the UNESCO review warns that, because of storage effects, it may take several decades for basins larger than several hundred square kilometres before stream sediment loads downstream become noticeably smaller, and its sediment statement is a review judgement, not a measurement [ev_sediment_retention_bruij90_14, ev_sediment_retention_bruij90_13]. The Chinese evidence carries its own nulls: in the Three-Gorge Reservoir Area vegetation and engineering measures together contributed 12.1–13.9% sediment reduction, so the vegetation share should be less than 10% in most instances [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_2]; decreased Pearl River sediment loads had little to do with soil conservation measures in the past 20 years [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_3]; and a four-year measurement in 12 small Loess Plateau watersheds found an inversely decreasing trend of erosion reduction with vegetation cover and attributed it to the immaturity of the planted species [ev_erosion_hazard_ran13_4]. A Himalayan position paper judges that reforestation will not likely have significant beneficial impact on soil loss [ev_erosion_hazard_ives87_1]. The Slovak result is modelled, runoff and sediment enter as components of erosion risk, and the Ethiopian runoff measurements are the only evidence from a low-income setting [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_2]. Plantation results, including the warnings that dense planted monocultures without understorey or litter can raise erosion, sit in the plantation family's erosion row, out of this row and the roll-up.

A meta-analysis from Ethiopia finds areas closed for grazing and agriculture had runoff coefficients of 4% against 19% on control sites [ev_runoff_reduction_meaza22_1], and in Leyte, Philippines, recovering forest on former slash-and-burn land generated the smallest share of overland flow among the land uses compared [ev_runoff_reduction_sidle06_1]. On harvested slopes, the higher probability of landslides following timber removal diminishes substantially 15–25 yr after harvesting as replacement trees mature [ev_erosion_hazard_sidle06_2], and a global forest-water assessment adds that land abandonment with expanding forest and grassland has in some cases decreased soil erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_iufro18_5].
conditionality: The same global assessment reports that abandoned land in previously terraced landscapes is particularly prone to gully erosion and landslides [ev_erosion_hazard_iufro18_4]. effect_mechanism: The plantation evidence points both ways, so no direction is stated. Under good tree cover erosion falls: in eucalyptus afforestation in Calabria, Italy, sediment concentrations were substantially greater on a plot with little or no tree cover, confirming the importance of the forest canopy in reducing erosion [ev_erosion_hazard_porto09_1]. In New Zealand, converting pasture to production forest cuts landslide erosion: in the Waipaoa catchment, calculated landsliding for 1990 and 1995 conditions suggests reforestation over that period produced a 10% decrease in sediment from landslides, equivalent to a 2% decrease in suspended load, and a scenario reforesting the 66 km2 of pasture in the most susceptible areas would cut landslide sediment inputs by 20% [ev_erosion_hazard_reidpage03_1, ev_erosion_hazard_reidpage03_4]; a national model finds new radiata pine forests, once mature, generally reduce mass-movement erosion by an order of magnitude [ev_erosion_hazard_dymond12_1]. Erosion can also worsen under plantations: particularly serious erosion problems arise in plantations where the soil has been cleared of vegetation and litter to reduce fire hazard or where litter is collected for livestock bedding or fuel [ev_erosion_hazard_faocifor05_3], and an FAO synthesis names dense, planted monocultures with little or no understorey and ground cover as experiencing increased surface erosion rates [ev_erosion_hazard_ham08_4].
conditionality: What separates the sides is the erosion process and the ground layer under the trees. The gains are on mass movement and on erosion where canopy and cover are good: mature stands reinforce slopes against landslides, and sediment falls under good tree cover [ev_erosion_hazard_dymond12_1, ev_erosion_hazard_reidpage03_1, ev_erosion_hazard_porto09_1]. The losses are surface erosion where understorey, vegetation and litter are absent, cleared or collected [ev_erosion_hazard_faocifor05_3, ev_erosion_hazard_ham08_4]. The actionable reading is a management condition, keeping understorey and litter, rather than a property of plantations as such. Both loss statements come from syntheses rather than measurements and state no comparator, and the gain side is a high-income Italian catchment study and New Zealand models: the Waipaoa calculation assumes a lower landslide frequency under forest, its targeting result is a scenario, and the national model's benefit applies once forests are mature and pauses after harvest while roots decay [ev_erosion_hazard_reidpage03_1, ev_erosion_hazard_reidpage03_4, ev_erosion_hazard_dymond12_1]. The plantation family is parked out of the forest-restoration roll-up and this row is published on its own: read it as evidence about plantations, not about restoration toward a natural baseline. A global meta-analysis found plantations gave 60.6% less erosion control than reference native forests [ev_erosion_hazard_hua22_1]; that compares plantations with natural forest, not with the land planted, so it is held out of the rating.
